opus-5.5.text:
I think what ultimately matters is whether you really care about the thing you're building, and whether you enjoy the process of building it, not just the outcome.

When I look back on projects like XGBoost or TVM, very few of them went the way I originally imagined. At the beginning you have a vague idea that something could be useful. Then you hit a lot of walls: things don't work, people don't pay attention, and sometimes you wonder whether you're going in the right direction at all. If the only thing keeping you going is the expectation of a specific result, like a paper or recognition, those setbacks can be really discouraging, because you can't control those outcomes.

What you can control is how you approach each day. Are you learning something? Are you solving a problem you find interesting? Are you making the thing a bit better than yesterday? I've found that if I focus on that, the setbacks become part of the journey instead of a verdict on whether I've succeeded or failed.

The other part is people. A lot of what kept those projects alive was the community: collaborators, students, and users who found the work useful and contributed back. When you're working with people you trust and respect, the uncertainty feels much less scary, because you're figuring it out together.

So for me it comes down to genuine interest in the problem, the joy of building, continuous learning, and the people you go on the journey with. The outcomes are unpredictable, and sometimes the most impactful thing comes out of a direction you didn't expect. If you keep those core things, you'll usually end up somewhere meaningful, even if it's not where you first planned to go.

r001.rationale: The response says what ultimately matters is caring about the project and enjoying the process of building it, even when setbacks and unpredictable outcomes arise.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what ultimately matters is whether you still care about the problem once the outcome stops cooperating with your plan.

When I started working on XGBoost, it wasn't the project I expected to define that period of my life. It began as a side effort, something I built because I needed a faster tree learner for a competition and the tools at the time didn't do what I wanted. There were many points where it would have been reasonable to stop. It wasn't publishable in the way my advisors would have preferred, there was no guarantee anyone would use it, and for a while the only users were me and a handful of people on a forum. Later, with TVM and MXNet, we hit different kinds of setbacks: hardware changing under us, design decisions we had to throw away, competing systems with far more resources.

What I learned is that you can't control the outcome, and trying to optimize directly for it tends to make you fragile. If I had been working on XGBoost only for the recognition, the long quiet stretch would have killed it. What kept it alive was that the technical question itself was interesting to me: how do you make gradient boosting both fast and correct on real, messy data? Setbacks on that question weren't failures, they were just information about where the hard part actually was.

So the practical answer is: pick problems where the process of working on them is rewarding on its own, and be honest about your assumptions so you can update them quickly. Treat each setback as a signal about the structure of the problem rather than a verdict on yourself. And build in the open with other people, because a community will carry something through the periods where your own motivation dips.

The unforeseeable part is real, and I don't think you can engineer it away. But if the work has substance, surprises tend to be more often good than bad. Many of the things I'm most proud of came from directions I didn't plan. The job is to stay in a position where you can notice them when they arrive.

r001.rationale: The response says to choose problems where the process of working on them is rewarding on its own, and describes sustained interest in the technical question as what kept the project going through setbacks.

astra-6.text: I think what ultimately matters is whether you still believe the endeavor is worth pursuing, and whether you’re learning along the way. You can put a lot of effort into something and still get an outcome you didn’t expect. That doesn’t necessarily mean the effort was wasted. The important thing is to be honest about what didn’t work, stay open to changing your approach, and decide what’s worth trying next. Persistence matters, but it should leave room for you to learn.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes believing the endeavor is worth pursuing and learning from setbacks, but it does not identify enjoying the process as what ultimately matters.

sol-6.1.text: I think what ultimately matters is whether you find the endeavor meaningful and whether you keep learning along the way. You can make a careful plan, but you can’t control every outcome. When something doesn’t work, you have to ask what it teaches you and what you should change. That might mean trying again, or it might mean taking a different approach. Persistence matters, but so does being willing to revise your assumptions. Even when the result is different from what you hoped for, the understanding you gain and the people you work with can make the effort worthwhile.

r001.rationale: The response says meaning, learning, and the people involved can make the effort worthwhile, but it does not identify enjoying the process as what ultimately matters.
